description: Baku-based team building an AI-powered predictive tool that harmonizes MODIS and VIIRS hot spot data into one reliable fire picture. Looking for teammates in data/AI, development and design.
summary: ODLAR combines 25 years of NASA MODIS and VIIRS active fire detections into one consistent record for 27,092 districts in 193 countries. Because the sensors differ in resolution and sensitivity, merging their detections makes fire activity appear to grow with each new satellite: in the raw data it rises in 99% of the 175 countries with enough fires. We bring the MODIS years onto the VIIRS scale with quantile mapping by region and season, estimate the fires MODIS missed, and give every corrected week an uncertainty range. In leave-one-year-out tests, raw MODIS counts are 75% below VIIRS, while the corrected values are typically within 1.3%. After correction, the 99% falls to 23%. On this record we built district fire calendars and 7-day and 13-week machine learning forecasts. Updated daily, the record has continued since Suomi NPP stopped sending data in November 2026. The Global Fire Monitoring Center (GFMC) in Freiburg looked at ODLAR and called such a record and calendar "absolutely useful" for monitoring fires, regulating fire use on farmland and preventing wildfires. It also noted that land cover is needed to separate agricultural burning from wildfires. Adding it is our next step. Everything is at https://odlar.app/
details:
The name ODLAR means "fires" in Azerbaijani, and Azerbaijan is often called the Land of Fire. We started from our own country, where raw satellite counts suggest that fire activity has grown by about 82% per decade since 2001. NASA's active fire archive is one of the longest global records of fire, but it is built from different instruments. MODIS on Terra (since 2000) and Aqua (since 2002) observes fires with 1 km pixels, while VIIRS on Suomi NPP (since 2012), NOAA-20 (since 2018) and NOAA-21 (since 2024) uses 375 m pixels and detects many small fires that MODIS cannot see. Every time a new instrument enters the archive, the number of detections jumps. If the data are used as they are, fire activity appears to rise almost everywhere: the raw trend for 2001 to 2025 is positive in 173 of the 175 countries that have enough fires to measure a trend (at least 500 detections over the period), and the global trend is about 94% per decade. The other 18 of the 193 countries have too few fires for a reliable trend. Most of this rise comes from the change of sensors and not from what happens on the ground. The question is also becoming practical, because MODIS will be retired in 2027 and Suomi NPP has already stopped sending fire data.

ODLAR downloads the complete FIRMS archive for all five instruments, using the science-quality archive where it exists and near real-time data for the most recent months. After cleaning, the record contains more than 500 million detections. We keep only detections classified as presumed vegetation fires and remove those with low confidence. Gas flares and other industrial heat sources are removed as well; in near real-time data, which carry no source type, we recognize them as small cells that stay hot month after month. The detections are then counted per day and per week for 27,092 districts in 193 countries, using administrative boundaries from OpenStreetMap and geoBoundaries. For weather we use NASA POWER for the historical period and Open-Meteo for the latest days and the 7-day forecast.

The harmonized record is expressed on the scale of VIIRS Suomi NPP. From January 2012 the record is the Suomi NPP observation itself, and the earlier MODIS years are converted to this scale using relations learned from the years when both instruments were operating. For weeks in which MODIS detected fire in a district, we use empirical quantile mapping fitted separately for each region and season, followed by a correction that depends on the size of the MODIS count. Districts with fewer than 12 fire weeks use the mapping of their country. Quantile mapping cannot deal with weeks in which MODIS saw nothing, even though VIIRS often detects small fires in such weeks. In Azerbaijan, for example, 25% of Suomi NPP detections between 2013 and 2024 fell in weeks when MODIS recorded no fire at all. For these weeks we fit a logistic regression that estimates the probability that VIIRS would have seen fire, based on the time of year, activity in the neighboring weeks and activity in the rest of the country, and multiply it by the average count of such weeks. The years before July 2002, when only Terra was available, are treated separately because Aqua added a second set of daily overpasses. Uncertainty is estimated with a block bootstrap over years (200 replicates), which gives every corrected week and year a 90% interval.

We validated the correction in three ways. In a leave-one-year-out test, each overlap year is removed in turn, the model is fitted on the remaining years, and the corrected MODIS values are compared with the real VIIRS values of the removed year. Raw MODIS counts are 75% below VIIRS in this test, while the corrected record is typically within 1.3% (median over our 180 regional batches). In the South Caucasus pilot, the weekly 90% intervals contained the observed value in 94% of cases. Second, we applied the Pettitt change-point test to the national series. In the raw data, 168 of 175 countries show a break, 157 of them in the years when Suomi NPP or NOAA-20 entered the record. After correction, 72 countries show a break and only 28 of these fall in those years. Third, as an independent check, we calculated trends from MODIS alone for 2003 to 2025, a series that never mixes sensors. These trends have the same sign as ODLAR in 156 of 175 countries. Globally, MODIS alone gives a decline of about 10% per decade and ODLAR a decline of 9.5%, while the raw archive shows the increase of 94% mentioned above. For Azerbaijan, MODIS alone shows a decline of 21% per decade and ODLAR a decline of 26%. The correction does not erase real changes: Canada (46% per decade) and India (11% per decade) still show significant increases.

Suomi NPP, the reference satellite of our record, stopped sending fire data on 2 November 2026. Since then the record continues from NOAA-20, scaled by a ratio between the two instruments that is learned for each region and season from the two years before the outage. Regions with few fires borrow the ratio of their country. To test this, we hid a real 16-month period of Suomi NPP data, from July 2025 to October 2026, and rebuilt it from NOAA-20. The reconstruction was 5.6% below the real values worldwide. Because the record is defined on the VIIRS scale, it does not depend on MODIS and will continue after MODIS is switched off.

From the harmonized record we build a fire calendar for every district. It shows when the fire season usually starts and ends (the weeks by which 10% and 90% of a year's activity has occurred), which weeks are critical (above the 75th percentile), and whether the current week, month or year is unusual compared with the district's own history. A period is marked as unusual when it is at least two standard deviations above normal and at least 1.5 times the usual level, and we also flag seasons that start or end at least two weeks earlier or later than usual. In practice this answers the question "is this month normal here?", and the raw data can give the wrong answer. In July 2026, raw detections in Azerbaijan were 4.1 times the usual July, which would suggest an exceptional month, but on the harmonized scale activity was 0.6 times the usual level.

The forecasting part of ODLAR is trained on the harmonized record. For every district and day, a LightGBM classifier estimates the probability that the next 7 days will be an unusual fire week, meaning activity above the district's 75th percentile for the same time of year. The probabilities are calibrated with isotonic regression and grouped into five risk levels. A second LightGBM model with a Tweedie objective estimates the expected number of detections, and three quantile models (10th, 50th and 90th percentiles) give an outlook for the next 13 weeks. The models use 31 features: recent fire activity over several time windows, the district's climatology, the 7-day weather forecast, observed weather of the previous weeks, and location, elevation and season. For each forecast we show the main drivers using TreeSHAP values, so users can see whether the risk comes from recent fires, dry weather or the season. We evaluated the models with rolling-origin validation, always training on earlier years and testing on each year from 2020 to 2025. Trained on our record, the 7-day model reaches a Brier skill score of 0.17 relative to climatology, compared with 0.06 for the same model trained on raw counts (median over batches). In the South Caucasus pilot the ROC AUC is 0.86, against 0.72 for climatology. The difference between the two training sets lies mostly in calibration. In the same pilot, when the model trained on raw counts gave a probability of around 74%, the event happened in 49% of cases, while for the model trained on ODLAR it happened in 66%. We also looked back at a fire in Lachin district that burned from 27 November to 2 December 2025. A model trained only on earlier years put the district at the highest risk level (0.86) on 20 November, a week before the fire started. In these back-tests observed weather takes the place of the forecast, so the skill in real operation will be somewhat lower.

All of this is available in a web application at https://odlar.app/ in Azerbaijani and English. Users can explore fire detections on an interactive map with daily NASA GIBS satellite imagery, open any district to see its fire calendar and current risk, compare the raw and harmonized series in our Harmonization Lab, read the methodology, and download the data as CSV or GeoJSON with uncertainty bounds or access it through an API. A simple mode presents the same information for the general public, and registered users can subscribe to risk alerts for their area, delivered in the application, by email or through Telegram. The record and the forecasts are refreshed every day from FIRMS. The data pipeline and the models are written in Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, LightGBM, GeoPandas, DuckDB) and served with FastAPI. A Laravel gateway with PostgreSQL and PostGIS handles accounts, caching, rate limits and an hourly alert check, and the frontend is built with Next.js, React, MapLibre GL and Tailwind CSS. We test the system with pytest, Pest, Vitest and Playwright, including automated accessibility checks. It runs with Docker Compose on a single cloud server and needs no special hardware.

We designed ODLAR with three groups of users in mind. Researchers need to know how far they can trust each number, so every corrected value comes with its uncertainty and the validation results are published in the application. Emergency services, fire managers and local authorities need probabilities they can act on, so the forecasts are calibrated and reported against a climatological baseline. The general public needs a clear answer in their own language, which is why we added the simple mode and the Azerbaijani interface.

During the hackathon we asked the Global Fire Monitoring Center (GFMC) in Freiburg, Germany, for feedback on ODLAR, and Johann G. Goldammer replied on behalf of the center. He wrote that a consistent long-term fire record and fire calendar is "absolutely useful" for monitoring fires in the South Caucasus and elsewhere, that it helps with planning the regulation of fire use on agricultural and pasture land and with preparedness for wildfire prevention and response, and he described our work as "very encouraging". He also named the most important missing piece, which is land and vegetation cover. Without it, management fires on farmland and pastures cannot be separated from wildfires in forests and protected areas, and it is not possible to see where carelessly applied agricultural fire spreads into fire-sensitive vegetation. Our next step is therefore to attach land cover from NASA's MODIS land cover product and protected area boundaries to every detection, so that the calendar and the forecasts can be read separately for cropland, pasture, forest and protected land.

Apart from land cover, there are other limitations we want to state openly. The forecast models were trained with observed weather in place of archived forecasts, vegetation greenness currently enters the model as a seasonal curve rather than satellite NDVI, and the harmonization assumes that the relation between the sensors in the overlap years also holds before 2012. In our view, the new part of ODLAR is how these pieces are combined. Instead of a single conversion factor between the sensors, we treat harmonization as a statistical problem, with corrections for each region and season, a separate model for missed fires, explicit uncertainty and out-of-sample validation. We then show that this matters for machine learning, since the same model gives much more reliable probabilities when it is trained on the harmonized record. The system has also already kept the record going through a real change of satellites.

We used Claude, an AI assistant made by Anthropic, through Claude Code during development. It helped us write, review and debug code, analyze data, and draft and translate texts and presentation material between Azerbaijani and English. The methods, design decisions and validation are our own, and every number in this description comes from our pipeline and validation runs. The statistical and machine learning models inside ODLAR (quantile mapping, logistic regression and LightGBM) were trained by us on NASA data and do not use generative AI. No AI-generated images, video or audio are used in the project.

The application is available at https://odlar.app/
